# Lesson Guide — Stuart Batty: Sharpening the Bowl Gouge
**Source:** Stuart Batty Woodturning (YouTube) | **Generated by:** The Crafters Hub AI Concierge  
**Date:** 2026-08-24 | **Confidence:** video_extract

---

## Technique
**Bowl Gouge Sharpening with a Platform Jig**

The fundamental skill every woodturner must master before touching a blank: achieving a consistent, repeatable grind on the bowl gouge that produces a flute-down cutting edge capable of clean, controlled shear cuts in endgrain and sidegrain bowls.

---

## At a Glance

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Category** | Woodturning |
| **Skill Level** | Intermediate |
| **Duration** | 20–30 minutes per session |
| **Outcome** | Consistently sharp bowl gouge with swept-back fingernail grind |

---

## Materials
- Bowl gouge blank (⅜" to ½" diameter)
- Water or oil (for wheel cooling)
- Marker (Sharpie) for checking grind

## Tools
- Slow-speed grinder (1750 RPM) — **not a high-speed bench grinder**
- 80-grit CBN (Cubic Boron Nitride) grinding wheel
- Wolverine Vari-Grind platform jig or equivalent
- Diamond honing card (for micro-bevel touch-up)
- Safety face shield (full-face, not glasses)

---

## Safety
> **CRITICAL — Read before touching the grinder:**
> - Always wear a **full-face shield**, not safety glasses. Grinding sparks travel upward.
> - Inspect the grinding wheel for cracks before every session. Tap with a wooden mallet — a cracked wheel rings dull, a good wheel rings clear.
> - Never grind a cold tool by pressing hard. Keep passes light and even — **overheating destroys the temper** of HSS steel and permanently ruins the tool edge.
> - Keep a water cup beside the grinder. Dip the tool every 3–5 seconds under load.
> - Never touch the grinding wheel surface with bare skin while it is spinning.

---

## Step-by-Step

1. **Mark the edge with a Sharpie.** Color the existing bevel completely. This shows you exactly where the wheel is removing metal on each pass — you want even removal across the full bevel width.

2. **Set your platform jig.** Adjust the Vari-Grind arm so the tool sits at a 40–45° angle to the wheel face. Lock the set screw. This angle determines your final bevel angle — shallower = longer bevel = stronger edge for finishing cuts.

3. **Set the flute position.** For a swept-back (Lady Fingernail) grind, rotate the tool so the flute faces 10 o'clock (viewed from the handle end). This is your starting position.

4. **Make the first pass — center of the edge.** With the grinder running, bring the tool to the wheel with very light pressure. Sweep from left to right using your whole upper body — not just your wrist. One smooth arc. Lift off before the end of the stroke.

5. **Check the Sharpie.** The marker should be gone where the wheel contacted. Gaps in the Sharpie reveal flat spots that need more work. Uneven removal means your pressure or speed was inconsistent.

6. **Sweep the wings.** Rotate the tool handle to the right (clockwise) while simultaneously swinging the tool across the wheel face. This creates the swept-back shape. Right wing: rotate handle right while sweeping left. Left wing: rotate handle left while sweeping right.

7. **Check the grind symmetry.** The edge profile viewed from the flute should be a smooth arc — no flat spots at the center, no uneven wings. The bevel should show a single consistent polish line across its full width.

8. **Hone the micro-bevel.** Take the diamond honing card and make 3–4 light strokes directly on the bevel. This removes the wire edge the grinder creates and produces a razor-sharp final edge. Do NOT hone the flute face.

9. **Test on scrap first.** Mount a piece of green or dry softwood and make a light shear cut. The gouge should cut cleanly without grabbing or chattering. Any catching means the grind is uneven or the bevel angle is too steep.

---

## Key Concepts

- **Bevel angle controls cut type.** 40° = aggressive cuts for roughing bowls. 55° = finishing cuts, more stable.
- **The bevel must ride the wood surface.** If the bevel is off the wood, the tool digs in (a "catch"). Learning to feel the bevel contact is the fundamental skill of woodturning.
- **CBN wheels stay cool.** Unlike aluminum oxide wheels, CBN (Cubic Boron Nitride) wheels remove metal without generating excessive heat. This preserves the HSS temper.
- **Swept-back grind vs. Irish grind.** Swept-back (fingernail) allows the turner to use the tip and wings independently — essential for bowl interiors. Irish grind (flat across) is simpler but less versatile.
- **Grinding is a learnable physical skill.** Consistency comes from repetition with a locked jig, not from "feeling" the angle freehand. Use a jig every time until the motion is muscle memory.

---

## Common Mistakes

1. **Grinding without a jig** — freehand grinding produces inconsistent bevel angles. Use a platform jig every time.
2. **Using a 3450 RPM grinder** — high-speed grinders overheat tools in seconds. Always use a slow-speed (1725–1800 RPM) grinder for turning tools.
3. **Pushing too hard on the wheel** — light, consistent pressure removes metal evenly. Heavy pressure creates flat spots and overheats.
4. **Forgetting to sweep the wings** — only grinding the center creates a flat-tipped gouge (spindle gouge profile), which causes catches on bowl interiors.
5. **Skipping the Sharpie test** — guessing the grind is complete without visual confirmation. Always use marker to verify full-bevel contact.
6. **Not cooling the tool** — dipping in water every 3–5 passes prevents heat discoloration. If the steel turns blue or purple, the temper is gone and the tool needs to be re-tempered or replaced.
